title: Role of Interfacial Coherency on Creep Behavior of FCC/BCC High-Entropy Alloy Multilayers.

recollection.starting_material: Alternating multilayers of FCC and BCC high-entropy alloy films (e.g., FCC CoCrFeNi vs. BCC NbMoTaW) deposited on a substrate
recollection.intervention: Systematic variation of individual layer thickness (≈2–50 nm) to tune the coherency/misfit of the FCC/BCC interfaces, followed by high-temperature constant-stress creep tests
recollection.structure: Nanoscale superlattice with either fully coherent, semi-coherent, or incoherent FCC/BCC interfaces depending on layer thickness; dislocation arrays or misfit dislocations form at semi-coherent interfaces
recollection.mechanism: Creep accommodated by dislocation glide and climb confined in individual layers; coherent interfaces act as strong barriers, forcing dislocations to bow or climb, while incoherent interfaces allow easier transmission; thus creep rate rises as coherency is lost
recollection.results: Guess: at 800 °C and 100 MPa, coherent 5 nm/5 nm multilayers show a minimum creep rate of ~10⁻⁹ s⁻¹, whereas 25 nm/25 nm semi-coherent multilayers exhibit ~10⁻⁷ s⁻¹; activation energy for creep increases from ~280 kJ mol⁻¹ (incoherent) to ~360 kJ mol⁻¹ (coherent)

score.note: The recollection correctly identifies layer-thickness variation as a way to tune coherent versus semicoherent interfaces and correctly mentions misfit dislocations at semicoherent interfaces. However, it gives the wrong alloy system, thickness range, and creep-test method. Its mechanism reverses the paper’s interpretation: coherent interfaces transmit dislocations more readily, while semicoherent M16 interfaces strongly block them and may promote interfacial amorphization-assisted diffusion/interface slip. All temperatures, stresses, creep rates, activation energies, and thickness-specific rankings are fabricated and inconsistent with the nanoindentation results.
